title: Being hillbilly musicians and seeking the respect of other musicians
summary: Parker says the band was painfully aware of its hillbilly label and strove for acceptance from musicians. He rates the Doughboys the best-playing band of the thirties and mentions a Gene Autry film.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: During this time, did you consider yourself to be a hillbilly musician?
Yes, yes. And we were painfully aware of that fact and always have been. I know this is a strong motivation behind our wanting to excel and wanting acceptance, the status symbol. It's powerful here.
Who did you want acceptance by?
The musicians primarily. And if any music, it's that same old idea of the carving contest and the same idea down in New Orleans, you want the musicians to accept you.

Any musicians that happen to be around. Let some musicians come on the scene and somehow we spot them out there and trot out our finest stuff. Used to be a W.E.O. Daniels had a band about the same time. And whenever at church, whenever at state fairs or big conventions we'd be playing together, we were always very careful to use only our best material when we saw them lurking in the sidelines. And we had a quality of it too, there's no doubt about it. The Dubois band, I think, undoubtedly, was the, oh, from the standpoint of musicianship, the very best of them all in the thirties.

Now you tell me what, now it's time, you tell me what others, compare the, if you would, do you recall the records made in the thirties and all with these other bands? Oh, no. No. We were the only ones who'd made a picture with Gene Autry, old Susanna. Did you know about that? No.
